title: How Do We Know Matthew Was a Tax Collector?
paragraphs:
How Do We Know Matthew Was a Tax Collector?
The Man Everyone Hated… Until Jesus Called Him
Some scandals never leave a person.
You can repent.
You can change.
You can dedicate your life to God.
And still, there will always be people who remember who you used to be.
Matthew knew exactly what that felt like.
Long before his name was attached to one of the four Gospels that would change the world forever, he was known for something very different.
He was a tax collector.
Not a pastor.
Not a disciple.
Not an apostle.
Not a Gospel writer.
A tax collector.
And in first-century Judea, that title carried a weight many modern readers fail to understand.
Tax collectors were viewed as traitors.

They worked for the Roman Empire, the occupying force that ruled over Israel. Many collected more money than required and kept the excess for themselves. They became wealthy through a system many Jews considered corrupt and oppressive.
To the average Jewish family, tax collectors were not simply disliked.
They were despised.
They represented compromise.
Collaboration.
Greed.
Betrayal.
If there was a list of people least likely to become one of God's chosen messengers, Matthew's name would have been near the top.
Yet that is exactly why his story still shakes hearts two thousand years later.
Because the Gospel is not the story of good people finding God.
It is the story of God finding people everyone else has already written off.
But how do we actually know Matthew was a tax collector?
The answer begins in Scripture itself.
In Matthew 9:9, the apostle records:
"As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, 'Follow me.' And he rose and followed him."
The phrase translated "tax booth" comes from the Greek expression:
"ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον" (epi to telōnion)
The word "τελώνιον" (telōnion) refers specifically to a tax office, customs station, or place where duties and tolls were collected.
Matthew was not merely near a tax office.
He was sitting at it.
Working.
Collecting.
Doing the very job that made him notorious among his own people.
The evidence becomes even stronger when we compare the parallel accounts.
Mark 2:14 states:
"And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, 'Follow me.'"
Luke 5:27 similarly records:
"After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth."
Many scholars recognize Levi and Matthew as the same person.
This was not uncommon in the ancient world. Jewish individuals frequently had multiple names.
Just as Simon became Peter.
Just as Saul became Paul.
Levi was also known as Matthew.
Notice something important.
Mark and Luke explicitly identify him as a tax collector.
Matthew's own Gospel simply states that he was sitting at the tax booth.
This subtle detail is fascinating.
Rather than emphasizing his former occupation, Matthew's account is actually more restrained than the others.
There is no attempt to glorify his past.
No effort to soften it.
No self-defense.
Just honesty.
The story stands as it happened.
And perhaps that humility itself becomes evidence of authenticity.
People inventing heroic legends tend to elevate themselves.
Matthew does the opposite.
He lets the other Gospel writers reveal what he used to be.
Then Scripture provides another powerful clue.
Immediately after Jesus called him, Matthew hosted a large gathering.
Matthew 9:10 says:
"And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples."
Why were so many tax collectors present?
Because they were Matthew's circle.
His coworkers.
His associates.
His community.
People usually gather with those they know.
Matthew's guest list quietly confirms what his profession had been.
Yet the greatest proof may not be historical.
It may be theological.
Because Matthew's Gospel bears the fingerprints of someone familiar with numbers, records, accounting, and precise details.
Tax collectors handled financial transactions daily.
They tracked figures.
Recorded obligations.
Calculated duties.
Organized information.
Many scholars have observed that Matthew's Gospel often displays structured organization and careful arrangement, characteristics consistent with someone accustomed to record keeping.
While this does not prove the case by itself, it harmonizes remarkably well with the testimony of the Gospels.
But perhaps the bigger question is not whether Matthew was a tax collector.
The bigger question is why Jesus chose him.
Why not a priest?
Why not a respected scholar?
Why not someone with a spotless reputation?
Because Jesus was revealing something about the Kingdom of God.
Something humanity still struggles to believe.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a God who specializes in redemption.
The prophet Isaiah declares:
"Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18).
The Hebrew word for scarlet is "שָׁנִי" (shani), a vivid crimson stain.
The image is intentional.
Deep guilt.
Visible guilt.
Permanent-looking guilt.
Yet God promises cleansing.
Transformation.
Restoration.
Not because sin is small.
But because grace is greater.
This truth reaches its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
When religious leaders criticized Him for eating with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus answered:

"Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners." (Matthew 9:12-13)
The word translated mercy echoes the Hebrew concept "חֶסֶד" (chesed).
Covenant love.
Steadfast love.
Faithful mercy.
A love that remains when everyone else walks away.
A love stronger than scandal.
A love stronger than shame.
A love stronger than your worst chapter.
That is why Matthew's story continues to resonate today.
Because every reader eventually discovers they have something in common with him.
Maybe you never sat at a tax booth.
Maybe you never worked for an occupying empire.
Maybe your scandal looks completely different.
But every person knows what it feels like to wish they could rewrite part of their story.
A failed marriage.
A hidden addiction.
A season of rebellion.
A betrayal.
A compromise.
A decision that still haunts you.
Many people spend their lives trying to outrun their past.
Jesus does something different.
He walks directly into it.
Then He says the same two words He spoke to Matthew:
"Follow me."
Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you become worthy.
Not after everyone forgives you.
Now.
Today.
Exactly where you are.
Matthew stood up from a tax booth.
And history changed.
The man known for collecting taxes became a collector of souls.
The man associated with greed became an ambassador of grace.
The man many considered unclean became the author of a Gospel that has led countless people to salvation through Jesus Christ.
Only God writes stories like that.
Only God can take scandal and turn it into testimony.
Only God can transform a traitor into a disciple.
Only God can take the chapters you hope nobody reads and turn them into evidence of His mercy.
And maybe that is why Matthew never gets old.
Because his story is not ultimately about Matthew.
It is about Jesus.
The Savior who sees beyond reputations.
Beyond labels.
Beyond failures.
Beyond shame.
Beyond what others think.
He sees what His grace can create.
If this article stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself. Someone you know may be one encounter with Jesus away from a completely rewritten story.
What part of your past has Jesus been transforming?
Your testimony may become someone else's hope.

If you desire to glorify God through helping others encounter biblical truth, one practical way is to support and share this ministry. Every share extends the reach of the Gospel beyond what we could accomplish alone.
The same Jesus who called Matthew is still calling people everyone else has already counted out.
